claim: The missense T300A variant in the core autophagy gene Atg16l1 is linked with increased risk for IBD.
source: Genome-wide association studies linked the missense T300A variant in the core autophagy gene Atg16l1 with increased risk for IBD (Hampe et al., 2007; Rioux et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published genome-wide association studies (Hampe et al., 2007; Rioux et al., 2007).

claim: The T300A variant in Atg16l1 contributes to enhanced caspase-mediated degradation of the ATG16L1 protein.
source: Later studies demonstrated that this variant contributes to enhanced caspase-mediated degradation of the ATG16L1 protein (Lassen et al., 2014; Murthy et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies that demonstrated this mechanism (Lassen et al., 2014; Murthy et al., 2014).

claim: Genetic loss-of-function of core autophagy genes including Atg16l1 increases secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines by macrophages in response to toll-like receptor (TLR) activation.
source: Genetic loss-of-function of core autophagy genes including Atg16l1 increases secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines by macrophages in response to toll-like receptor (TLR) activation (Lim et al., 2019; Saitoh et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this effect (Lim et al., 2019; Saitoh et al., 2008).

claim: Loss of Atg16l1 contributes to increased mucosal inflammation, driving resistance to extracellular pathogens such as Citrobacter rodentium.
source: This contributes to increased mucosal inflammation, driving resistance to extracellular pathogens such as Citrobacter rodentium (Marchiando et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2018) and pathogenic Escherichia coli (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing resistance to these pathogens (Marchiando et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).

claim: Loss of Atg16l1 contributes to increased mucosal inflammation, driving resistance to pathogenic Escherichia coli.
source: This contributes to increased mucosal inflammation, driving resistance to extracellular pathogens such as Citrobacter rodentium (Marchiando et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2018) and pathogenic Escherichia coli (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study showing resistance to E. coli (Wang et al., 2019).

claim: Loss of autophagy-related genes Atg16l1, Beclin1, and Rbc1cc1 in the myeloid compartment confers enhanced antimicrobial immunity against Salmonella typhimurium via induction of type I and II interferon responses.
source: Loss of autophagy-related genes Atg16l1, Beclin1, and Rbc1cc1 (encoding FIP200) in the myeloid compartment also confers enhanced antimicrobial immunity against certain intracellular pathogens, such as Salmonella typhimurium (S.typhimurium) and Listeria monocytogenes via induction of type I and II interferon responses (Samie et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this mechanism (Samie et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020).

claim: Loss of autophagy-related genes Atg16l1, Beclin1, and Rbc1cc1 in the myeloid compartment confers enhanced antimicrobial immunity against Listeria monocytogenes via induction of type I and II interferon responses.
source: Loss of autophagy-related genes Atg16l1, Beclin1, and Rbc1cc1 (encoding FIP200) in the myeloid compartment also confers enhanced antimicrobial immunity against certain intracellular pathogens, such as Salmonella typhimurium (S.typhimurium) and Listeria monocytogenes via induction of type I and II interferon responses (Samie et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this mechanism (Samie et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020).

claim: Xenophagy functions to eliminate intracellular bacteria by sequestering them in autophagosomes and shuttling them to the degradative lysosomal compartment.
source: In contrast to non-selective autophagy triggered by nutrient stress, xenophagy functions to eliminate intracellular bacteria by sequestering them in autophagosomes and shuttling them to the degradative lysosomal compartment.
evidence: The claim describes the established mechanism of xenophagy, drawing from scientific knowledge.

claim: S.typhimurium and S.flexneri have evolved mechanisms to evade capture by the autophagy machinery.
source: Pathogenic bacteria have evolved mechanisms to either evade capture by the autophagy machinery, as by S.typhimurium and S.flexneri (Birmingham et al., 2006; Campbell-Valois et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019b) or attenuate autophagic flux as by Legionella pneumophila (Choy et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating evasion mechanisms (Birmingham et al., 2006; Campbell-Valois et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019b).

claim: Legionella pneumophila attenuates autophagic flux.
source: Pathogenic bacteria have evolved mechanisms to either evade capture by the autophagy machinery, as by S.typhimurium and S.flexneri (Birmingham et al., 2006; Campbell-Valois et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019b) or attenuate autophagic flux as by Legionella pneumophila (Choy et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this mechanism (Choy et al., 2012).

claim: S.typhimurium primarily resides in a protective compartment known as the Salmonella containing vacuole (SCV).
source: S.typhimurium primarily resides in a protective compartment known as the Salmonella containing vacuole (SCV).
evidence: The claim describes established knowledge about S.typhimurium's intracellular lifestyle.

claim: S.typhimurium prevents formation of the ATG5~ATG12-ATG16L1 complex at the bacterial vacuolar membrane via secretion of the effector SopF.
source: There it prevents formation of the ATG5~ATG12-ATG16L1 complex at the bacterial vacuolar membrane via secretion of the effector SopF, which blocks ATG16L1 association with vacuolar ATPases (Xu et al., 2019b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this mechanism (Xu et al., 2019b).

claim: SopF blocks ATG16L1 association with vacuolar ATPases.
source: There it prevents formation of the ATG5~ATG12-ATG16L1 complex at the bacterial vacuolar membrane via secretion of the effector SopF, which blocks ATG16L1 association with vacuolar ATPases (Xu et al., 2019b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this mechanism (Xu et al., 2019b).

claim: Infected host cells recognize 10–20% of cytosolic S.typhimurium and subject this subpopulation to lysosomal degradation.
source: Despite its ability to interfere with autophagy, infected host cells still recognize 10–20% of cytosolic S.typhimurium and subject this subpopulation to lysosomal degradation via mechanisms involving direct recognition of either the bacterial surface (Huang and Brumell, 2014; Stolz et al., 2014) or damaged phagocytic membranes (Fujita et al., 2013; Thurston et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating these recognition mechanisms (Huang and Brumell, 2014; Stolz et al., 2014; Fujita et al., 2013; Thurston et al., 2012).

claim: S.flexneri resides in the host cytoplasm.
source: Compared to S.typhimurium, S.flexneri is not characterized by a vacuolar life cycle, but instead resides in the host cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim describes established knowledge about S.flexneri's intracellular lifestyle.

claim: S.flexneri effector proteins IcsB and VirA are capable of completely inhibiting autophagic recognition to permit replication in the host cytosol.
source: S.flexneri effector proteins IcsB and VirA are capable of completely inhibiting autophagic recognition to permit replication in the host cytosol (Liu et al., 2018; Ogawa et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this mechanism (Liu et al., 2018; Ogawa et al., 2005).

claim: The host cell attempts to counteract S.flexneri infection by coating bacterial cell surfaces with guanylate-binding proteins (GBPs).
source: In response, the host cell attempts to further counteract S.flexneri infection via diverse mechanisms, such as coating bacterial cell surfaces with guanylate-binding proteins (GBPs) (Li et al., 2017; Wandel et al., 2017) or sequestering bacteria in Septin cage-like structures to restrict their motility (Mostowy et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this mechanism (Li et al., 2017; Wandel et al., 2017).

claim: The host cell attempts to counteract S.flexneri infection by sequestering bacteria in Septin cage-like structures to restrict their motility.
source: In response, the host cell attempts to further counteract S.flexneri infection via diverse mechanisms, such as coating bacterial cell surfaces with guanylate-binding proteins (GBPs) (Li et al., 2017; Wandel et al., 2017) or sequestering bacteria in Septin cage-like structures to restrict their motility (Mostowy et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this mechanism (Mostowy et al., 2010).

claim: Loss of Atg16l1 in murine bone-marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) enhanced S.flexneri elimination in cell culture.
source: We observed that loss of Atg16l1 in murine bone-marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) enhanced S.flexneri elimination in cell culture, as well as by mice lacking ATG16L1 in the myeloid compartment (Atg16l1-cKO; LysM-Cre-mediated deletion of Atg16l1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Mice lacking ATG16L1 in the myeloid compartment (Atg16l1-cKO) enhanced S.flexneri elimination.
source: We observed that loss of Atg16l1 in murine bone-marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) enhanced S.flexneri elimination in cell culture, as well as by mice lacking ATG16L1 in the myeloid compartment (Atg16l1-cKO; LysM-Cre-mediated deletion of Atg16l1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: ATG16L1 deficiency significantly upregulated proteins involved in the glutathione-mediated antioxidant response to compensate for elevated oxidative stress.
source: Quantitative multiplexed proteomics of murine bone marrow-derived macrophages revealed that ATG16L1 deficiency significantly upregulated proteins involved in the glutathione-mediated antioxidant response to compensate for elevated oxidative stress, which simultaneously promoted S.flexneri killing.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data from the study.

claim: Elevated oxidative stress in ATG16L1-deficient macrophages simultaneously promoted S.flexneri killing.
source: Quantitative multiplexed proteomics of murine bone marrow-derived macrophages revealed that ATG16L1 deficiency significantly upregulated proteins involved in the glutathione-mediated antioxidant response to compensate for elevated oxidative stress, which simultaneously promoted S.flexneri killing.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data and functional assays from the study.

claim: Myeloid-specific deletion of Atg16l1 in mice accelerated bacterial clearance in vitro and in vivo.
source: Consistent with this, myeloid-specific deletion of Atg16l1 in mice accelerated bacterial clearance in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Pharmacological induction of oxidative stress through suppression of cysteine import enhanced microbial clearance by macrophages.
source: Pharmacological induction of oxidative stress through suppression of cysteine import enhanced microbial clearance by macrophages.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Antioxidant treatment of macrophages permitted S.flexneri proliferation.
source: Conversely, antioxidant treatment of macrophages permitted S.flexneri proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Control of oxidative stress by ATG16L1 and autophagy regulates antimicrobial immunity against intracellular pathogens.
source: These findings demonstrate that control of oxidative stress by ATG16L1 and autophagy regulates antimicrobial immunity against intracellular pathogens.
evidence: The claim is supported by the collective experimental data from the study.

claim: ATG16L1-deficient BMDMs (cKO) demonstrated enhanced bacterial clearance compared to wild type (WT) controls.
source: Compared to wild type (WT) controls, ATG16L1-deficient BMDMs (cKO) demonstrated enhanced bacterial clearance (Figure 1A and B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: WT and cKO BMDMs displayed similar cell death kinetics over the time course of infection.
source: WT and cKO BMDMs displayed similar cell death kinetics over the time course of infection, indicating that the phenotype was not driven by enhanced cell death, but potentially by other factors in cKO BMDMs (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The enhanced bacterial clearance phenotype in cKO BMDMs was not driven by enhanced cell death.
source: WT and cKO BMDMs displayed similar cell death kinetics over the time course of infection, indicating that the phenotype was not driven by enhanced cell death, but potentially by other factors in cKO BMDMs (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that cell death kinetics were similar between genotypes.

claim: Myeloid-specific loss of Atg16l1 resulted in a markedly decreased bacterial burden in the liver at 6 hr following infection.
source: However, myeloid-specific loss of Atg16l1 resulted in a markedly decreased bacterial burden in the liver (Figures 1D, 6 hr; Figures 1E, 24 hr).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Myeloid-specific loss of Atg16l1 resulted in a markedly decreased bacterial burden in the liver at 24 hr following infection.
source: However, myeloid-specific loss of Atg16l1 resulted in a markedly decreased bacterial burden in the liver (Figures 1D, 6 hr; Figures 1E, 24 hr).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ATG16L1 deficiency in macrophages enhances clearance of intracellular S.flexneri in vitro.
source: These findings indicate that ATG16L1 deficiency in macrophages enhances clearance of intracellular S.flexneri in vitro, while myeloid-specific loss of Atg16l1 accelerates hepatic clearance of S.flexneri in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Myeloid-specific loss of Atg16l1 accelerates hepatic clearance of S.flexneri in vivo.
source: These findings indicate that ATG16L1 deficiency in macrophages enhances clearance of intracellular S.flexneri in vitro, while myeloid-specific loss of Atg16l1 accelerates hepatic clearance of S.flexneri in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Quantitative data were obtained from >103,700 peptide features mapping to 9430 proteins in the global proteome profiling.
source: For global proteome profiling, quantitative data were obtained from >103,700 peptide features mapping to 9430 proteins.
evidence: The claim describes the quantitative results from the proteomic analysis.

claim: Quantitative data were obtained for >25,600 unique phospho-sites from 5052 proteins in the PTM enriched samples.
source: From the PTM enriched samples, quantitative data were obtained for >25,600 unique phospho- (5052 proteins) and >12,400 unique KGG(Ub)-sites (3324 proteins).
evidence: The claim describes the quantitative results from the PTM analysis.

claim: Quantitative data were obtained for >12,400 unique KGG(Ub)-sites from 3324 proteins in the PTM enriched samples.
source: From the PTM enriched samples, quantitative data were obtained for >25,600 unique phospho- (5052 proteins) and >12,400 unique KGG(Ub)-sites (3324 proteins).
evidence: The claim describes the quantitative results from the PTM analysis.

claim: The final dataset contained quantitative data for 7260 proteins, 9418 phospho-sites, and 3691 KGG(Ub)-sites when considering only features bearing data in both 11-plexes.
source: When considering only features bearing data in both 11-plexes, the final dataset contained quantitative data for 7260 proteins (i.e. global proteome), 9418 phospho- and 3691 KGG(Ub)-sites (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim describes the quantitative results from the proteomic analysis.

claim: ~90% of the post-translationally modified peptide spectral matches derived from proteins that were also identified and quantified in the global proteome dataset.
source: As expected, ~90% of the post-translationally modified peptide spectral matches derived from proteins that were also identified and quantified in the global proteome dataset (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Peptide and protein level quantitative data were highly reproducible, with Pearson correlations ranging from 0.96 to 0.99.
source: Both within and between plexes, peptide and protein level quantitative data were highly reproducible, with Pearson correlations ranging from 0.96 to 0.99 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: cKO BMDMs showed upregulation in autophagy receptors and inflammatory regulators, such as SQSTM/p62 and ZBP1.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Samie et al., 2018), cKO BMDMs showed upregulation in autophagy receptors and inflammatory regulators, such as SQSTM/p62 and ZBP1, respectively (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3A and is consistent with previous observations (Samie et al., 2018).

claim: Elevated phosphorylation of ubiquitin (RL40) at serine-57 (RL40_S57) was observed in cKO BMDMs.
source: In the phosphoproteome and KGG(Ub) datasets interesting observations concerned elevated phosphorylation of ubiquitin (RL40) at serine-57 (RL40_S57) (Figure 3B) and ubiquitination of FIS1 at lysine-20 (FIS1_K20) (Figure 3C), which are involved in endocytic trafficking (Lee et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2003) and mitochondrial and peroxisomal homeostasis (Bingol et al., 2014; Koch et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2012), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Elevated ubiquitination of FIS1 at lysine-20 (FIS1_K20) was observed in cKO BMDMs.
source: In the phosphoproteome and KGG(Ub) datasets interesting observations concerned elevated phosphorylation of ubiquitin (RL40) at serine-57 (RL40_S57) (Figure 3B) and ubiquitination of FIS1 at lysine-20 (FIS1_K20) (Figure 3C), which are involved in endocytic trafficking (Lee et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2003) and mitochondrial and peroxisomal homeostasis (Bingol et al., 2014; Koch et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2012), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Phosphorylation of ubiquitin at serine-57 is involved in endocytic trafficking.
source: In the phosphoproteome and KGG(Ub) datasets interesting observations concerned elevated phosphorylation of ubiquitin (RL40) at serine-57 (RL40_S57) (Figure 3B) and ubiquitination of FIS1 at lysine-20 (FIS1_K20) (Figure 3C), which are involved in endocytic trafficking (Lee et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2003) and mitochondrial and peroxisomal homeostasis (Bingol et al., 2014; Koch et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2012), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this function (Lee et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2003).

claim: Ubiquitination of FIS1 at lysine-20 is involved in mitochondrial and peroxisomal homeostasis.
source: In the phosphoproteome and KGG(Ub) datasets interesting observations concerned elevated phosphorylation of ubiquitin (RL40) at serine-57 (RL40_S57) (Figure 3B) and ubiquitination of FIS1 at lysine-20 (FIS1_K20) (Figure 3C), which are involved in endocytic trafficking (Lee et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2003) and mitochondrial and peroxisomal homeostasis (Bingol et al., 2014; Koch et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2012), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this function (Bingol et al., 2014; Koch et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2012).

claim: Global proteome analysis revealed broad changes in pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines at early (GROA), late (CXL10, IL1A, IL1B) or both (CCL2, TNFA) time-points.
source: For example, global proteome analysis revealed broad changes in pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines at early (GROA), late (CXL10, IL1A, IL1B) or both (CCL2, TNFA) time-points, as well as marked changes in several key cell surface receptors (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Tyrosine-431 of the PI3-kinase regulatory subunit (P85A_Y431) decreased rapidly upon infection in both genotypes.
source: For phosphorylation, notable examples included tyrosine-431 of the PI3-kinase regulatory subunit (P85A_Y431) which decreased rapidly upon infection in both genotypes, and S379 of the interferon regulatory factor (IRF3_S379) which was increased following infection, particularly in ATG16L1-deficient cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: S379 of the interferon regulatory factor (IRF3_S379) was increased following infection, particularly in ATG16L1-deficient cells.
source: For phosphorylation, notable examples included tyrosine-431 of the PI3-kinase regulatory subunit (P85A_Y431) which decreased rapidly upon infection in both genotypes, and S379 of the interferon regulatory factor (IRF3_S379) which was increased following infection, particularly in ATG16L1-deficient cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Marked effects were seen for the selective autophagy receptor Tax1BP1 (TAXB1_K618) and an E3 ubiquitin ligase Pellino (PELI1_K202) in ubiquitination analysis.
source: For ubiquitination, marked effects were seen for the selective autophagy receptor Tax1BP1 (TAXB1_K618) and an E3 ubiquitin ligase Pellino (PELI1_K202) (Figure 3F), both of which have defined roles at the intersection of cell death and innate immune signaling (Choi et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2011; Parvatiyar et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Tax1BP1 and Pellino have defined roles at the intersection of cell death and innate immune signaling.
source: For ubiquitination, marked effects were seen for the selective autophagy receptor Tax1BP1 (TAXB1_K618) and an E3 ubiquitin ligase Pellino (PELI1_K202) (Figure 3F), both of which have defined roles at the intersection of cell death and innate immune signaling (Choi et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2011; Parvatiyar et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating these roles (Choi et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2011; Parvatiyar et al., 2010).

claim: The global protein level of TAXB1 is elevated upon Atg16l1 deletion.
source: For TAXB1, these show that the global protein level is elevated upon Atg16l1 deletion, as are a number of individual phosphorylation and ubiquitination sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data from the study.

claim: A number of individual phosphorylation and ubiquitination sites on TAXB1 are elevated upon Atg16l1 deletion.
source: For TAXB1, these show that the global protein level is elevated upon Atg16l1 deletion, as are a number of individual phosphorylation and ubiquitination sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data from the study.

claim: Certain PTMs on TAXB1 such as phosphorylation at S632 and ubiquitination at K624 and K627 track with the protein level.
source: For TAXB1, certain PTMs such as phosphorylation at S632 and ubiquitination at K624 and K627 track with the protein, while other PTMs such as phosphorylation at threonine-494 (T494) and S693 display time-dependent changes that diverge from the underlying protein level (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Other PTMs on TAXB1 such as phosphorylation at threonine-494 (T494) and S693 display time-dependent changes that diverge from the underlying protein level.
source: For TAXB1, certain PTMs such as phosphorylation at S632 and ubiquitination at K624 and K627 track with the protein, while other PTMs such as phosphorylation at threonine-494 (T494) and S693 display time-dependent changes that diverge from the underlying protein level (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Genotype-dependent loss of each component of the ATG16L1-ATG5~ATG12 complex that conjugates LC3 (MLP3A) to phosphatidylethanolamine was confirmed.
source: We confirmed genotype-dependent loss of each component of the ATG16L1-ATG5~ATG12 complex that conjugates LC3 (MLP3A) to phosphatidylethanolamine (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Only modest changes were seen in the core autophagy machinery following infection, with the most notable effects being differential phosphorylation of FIP200 (RBCC1), ATG2B, and VPS15/p150 (PI3R4).
source: Only modest changes were seen in the core autophagy machinery following infection, with the most notable effects being differential phosphorylation of FIP200 (RBCC1), ATG2B, and VPS15/p150 (PI3R4) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: More substantial effects were seen for phosphorylation events on autophagy receptors such SQSTM/p62 and Optineurin (OPTN).
source: More substantial effects were seen for phosphorylation events on autophagy receptors such SQSTM/p62 and Optineurin (OPTN) (Figure 4E), in addition to TAXB1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4A.

claim: Singly and multiply phosphorylated forms of SQSTM/p62 at T269, T271, T272, S275/6, S277 were elevated in ATG16L1-deficient macrophages.
source: In the case of SQSTM/p62, singly and multiply phosphorylated forms of T269, T271, T272, S275/6, S277 were elevated in ATG16L1-deficient macrophages.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data from the study.

claim: S28 phosphorylation of SQSTM/p62 was previously described to regulate activation of the antioxidant response.
source: S28 phosphorylation of SQSTM/p62 was previously described to regulate activation of the antioxidant response (Xu et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this function (Xu et al., 2019a).

claim: A substantial increase in basal SQSTM_S28 phosphorylation was detected in cKO BMDMs.
source: We detected a substantial increase in basal SQSTM_S28 phosphorylation in cKO BMDMs, indicating that ATG16L1 deficiency may impact oxidative stress (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ATG16L1 deficiency may impact oxidative stress based on increased SQSTM_S28 phosphorylation.
source: We detected a substantial increase in basal SQSTM_S28 phosphorylation in cKO BMDMs, indicating that ATG16L1 deficiency may impact oxidative stress (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of increased SQSTM_S28 phosphorylation and its known role in antioxidant response.

claim: TBK1 regulates OPTN and SQSTM through phosphorylation.
source: Previous work from several groups have demonstrated that TBK1 regulates OPTN and SQSTM through phosphorylation, although the sites quantified in this dataset differ from those previously characterized in detail (Heo et al., 2015; Matsumoto et al., 2015; Richter et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this mechanism (Heo et al., 2015; Matsumoto et al., 2015; Richter et al., 2016).

claim: Ubiquitination on K278 of NEMO was detected, consistent with increased LUBAC activity.
source: For example, we detected ubiquitination on K278 of NEMO (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F), consistent with increased LUBAC activity (Tokunaga et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F and is consistent with previous observations (Tokunaga et al., 2009).

claim: A linear ubiquitin peptide derived from linear polyubiquitin chains formed by the LUBAC complex was elevated upon infection in both WT and cKO BMDMs.
source: Interestingly, the global proteome data reported a peptide with the sequence GGMQIFVK that is derived from linear polyubiquitin chains formed by the LUBAC complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). This linear ubiquitin peptide was elevated upon infection in both WT and cKO BMDMs, further supporting increased E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of LUBAC.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: TAXB1 phosphorylation was induced upon infection at a number of sites.
source: As noted above, TAXB1 phosphorylation was induced upon infection at a number of sites (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Changes in TAXB1 correlated with numerous elevated PTMs of the A20 (TNAP3) deubiquitinase.
source: These changes in TAXB1 correlated with numerous elevated PTMs of the A20 (TNAP3) deubiquitinase, a protein whose anti-inflammatory activity modulates NF-κB signaling (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: A20 (TNAP3) deubiquitinase has anti-inflammatory activity that modulates NF-κB signaling.
source: These changes in TAXB1 correlated with numerous elevated PTMs of the A20 (TNAP3) deubiquitinase, a protein whose anti-inflammatory activity modulates NF-κB signaling (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim describes established knowledge about A20's function.

claim: Phosphorylation at TAXB1 at S693 is important for the assembly of TNAP3-containing complex and negative regulation of NF-κB signaling.
source: Phosphorylation at TAXB1 at S693 is important for the assembly of TNAP3-containing complex and negative regulation of NF-κB signaling (Shembade et al., 2011; Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this function (Shembade et al., 2011).

claim: Notable changes were identified across numerous components implicated in pathogen sensing such as TLRs, RLRs, NLRs and STING/cGAS.
source: We also identified notable changes across numerous components implicated in pathogen sensing such as TLRs, RLRs, NLRs and STING/cGAS (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: The datasets confirm several previously demonstrated PTMs that occur in response to infection, such as elevated phosphorylation of RIPK1 at S321.
source: Our datasets confirm several previously demonstrated PTMs that occur in response to infection, such as elevated phosphorylation of RIPK1 at S321 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E), XIAP at S429 or IRF3 on multiple sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E and is consistent with previous observations.

claim: The datasets confirm elevated phosphorylation of XIAP at S429 in response to infection.
source: Our datasets confirm several previously demonstrated PTMs that occur in response to infection, such as elevated phosphorylation of RIPK1 at S321 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E), XIAP at S429 or IRF3 on multiple sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The datasets confirm elevated phosphorylation of IRF3 on multiple sites in response to infection.
source: Our datasets confirm several previously demonstrated PTMs that occur in response to infection, such as elevated phosphorylation of RIPK1 at S321 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E), XIAP at S429 or IRF3 on multiple sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: ABIN1 (TNIP1) showed modest changes in global protein levels, but elevated ubiquitination at multiple lysines including K360, K402, K480 at both timepoints and higher levels in cKO than WT.
source: Similar effects were observed for ABIN1 (TNIP1), which showed modest changes in global protein levels, but elevated ubiquitination at multiple lysines including K360, K402, K480 at both timepoints and higher levels in cKO than WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
